blocks: In this multi-disciplinary project a three-dimensional phase-field simulation was developed to study quantum dot growth kinetics and analyze the effects of anisotropic interfacial energy. The code was developed from a two-dimensional simulation written by J.J. Eggleston. Quantum dot kinetics with isotropic interfacial energy were analyzed and preliminary results of anisotropic interfacial energy are compared with their two-dimensional counterparts and are shown to be qualitatively similar. The three-dimensional implementation of anisotropic interfacial energy necessitated finding a regularized interfacial energy in three dimensions that enforces equilibrium at the corners of the facets and allows for cusp formation. In addition hardware-accelerated rendering software was developed to visualize three-dimensional simulation results, as well as models such as dendrite reconstructions. The software performs efficient curvature, surface normal, and lighting calculations and is optimized to handle multiple-frame progressions of a simulation, rendering real-time results in a virtual 3D environment.

Quantum dots are nano-scale structures which form from thin films deposited on a substrate by heteroepitaxy. It has been found that dots form to balance elastic strain energy due to lattice misfit between the film and the substrate and the increase in free energy associated with increasing surface area as the film forms dots. There is hope to use quantum dots in the upcoming shift from microelectronics to nanoelectronics because of their unique electrical, optical, and magnetic properties. When electrons are confined within a quantum dot they begin to take on discrete energy levels and act as quantum wells, making single-electron transistors possible.¹ The dots, which are on the order of about 100nm, may eventually be used as nano-scale switches in electronics because, like there microelectronic counterparts, they can connected (for example with carbon nanotubes) to form electronic circuits. Quantum dots play an important role in the study of spintronics where they can be used to make single-electron transistors, allowing for the design of devices at the quantum level.² Quantum computing has been proposed an may one day become a reality.³ It has been suggested that lattices of quantum dots and nanowires may be superconductive at high transition temperatures.⁴ Arrays of quantum dots have been
used to produce lasers,⁵ and metal quantum dots can hold distinct but recognizably unique magnetic domain patterns which make them good candidates for high-density computer memory.⁶

It is important to understand the shape and growth kinetics of quantum dots so they can be engineered to a specified size and placed in regularly repeating patterns for use in electronics. Current research is focusing on how to engineer large arrays of dots of a relatively uniform size and spatial distribution and to understand what factors control growth kinetics.

The aim of this project has been to develop and accurate model of interfaces for studying the growth kinetics of quantum dots forming from a thin film deposited on a substrate and determining the stress-free equilibrium shape of an isolated particle in a two-phase mixture in which there are preferred surface orientations due to surface energy anisotropy. The work is a continuation of a thesis written by J.J. Eggleston in 2001, in which he modeled 2D quantum-dot kinetics with both isotropic and anisotropic interfacial energy using a phase-field approach.⁷

The phase-field computational model is ideal for simulating quantum dots. The phase-field model, due to the fact that it models diffuse rather than explicit interfaces, avoids the complication of having to calculate surface integrals over the particle to calculate its total interfacial energy. Additionally, no explicit tracking of boundaries is necessary because the model uses chemical potential gradients and Cahn-Hilliard evolution to evolve the system.

In the phase-field model a variable φ from one phase to another. Because the transition occurs over a distance, the interface is a region with a finite width where φ changes rapidly – hence the phase-field method is based on a diffuse interface model. The diffuse interface model is an approximation for interfaces which has been adopted as a computational method for modeling solid surfaces. When the interfacial thickness is taken to be sufficiently small the diffuse interface description agrees with the classical description of an interface.
